tools.name: Covered-Call Monitor
tools.subtitle: returns, overlays and flows from SEC filings
tools.summary: What does the yield cost? For 87 US covered-call, buy-write and premium-income funds: the total return with distributions reinvested, beside an index fund where one applies and a mix with the same market risk, what each fund paid out, the options it had actually written, and the money moving in and out. Rebuilt every quarter from SEC filings.
tools.latest: 87 covered-call funds are followed. 18 of them can be set beside an index fund on the same market, and all 18 returned less than it, by 0.8 to 19.7 percentage points (median 5.5), distributions reinvested. The index funds returned 22% to 41% over these months: a market that rises this fast is where a cap on the upside costs most.
tools.caption: Five of the largest funds over three years, each beside its index fund.
tools.picture_alt: Total return over 3 years of 5 large covered-call funds, each beside the index fund on the same market
tools.paper: High Yield, Capped Gains: Mechanics, Trade-Offs, and Practical Diagnostics for Covered-Call ETFs
tools.paper_standing: peer-reviewed, The Journal of Beta Investment Strategies, 2026

tools.name: Crypto Observatory
tools.subtitle: required returns, risks and survival
tools.summary: What return should the holders of a cryptoasset require for the risks they carry? Recomputed every month from public data for Bitcoin, Ether, BNB, Solana and Tron, beside equities and gold: what each figure is made of, its Sharpe ratio and what volatility leaves of it. Bitcoin's requirement is tested against what it delivered since 2012, with the equation explained term by term and a census of cryptoasset deaths.
tools.latest: Bitcoin's required return is 18.8% a year: risk-free 4.9, market 5.8, concentration 6.2, mortality 1.9. Across the range of the model's inputs it runs from 11.7% to 25.9%. The same equation gives Ether 24.6%, BNB 17.3%, Solana 24.4%, Tron 9.1%, against 8.9% for the US stock market and 5.5% for gold. Each figure is the midpoint of its range. The paper's 18.1% for Bitcoin in 2026 is another measure of the same model: the median when all inputs are varied together.
tools.caption: What each required return is made of, with equities and gold priced the same way for scale.
tools.picture_alt: The required return of Bitcoin, Ether, BNB, Solana and Tron, each as a bar made of the risk-free rate, market risk, concentration risk and mortality risk, with three equity series and gold below for scale
tools.paper: Bitcoin's Required Return: Market Risk, Concentration and Mortality

tools.name: Dual-Risk DCF Calculator
tools.subtitle: the discount rate and the forecast, separated
tools.summary: Enter a benchmark rate and two views of the same asset, two forecasts or a forecast and a price, and the calculator puts the whole gap into one number, the valuation ratio K, with the gain of capital and the effective discount rate that follow from it. It also runs the same reading over your own price series. It computes in your browser and sends nothing out, and it runs as an MCP server for an AI assistant on your own machine.
tools.latest: a forecast 10% below the benchmark, at a benchmark rate of 8% over 5 years, gives a valuation ratio K of 1.111 and a gain of capital of +0.163. One discount rate would have to fall to 4.1% to hide the gap (5.7% by the article's closed form, which is exact for a single payoff).
tools.caption: A worked example: two forecasts of the same asset, valued at the same benchmark rate.
tools.picture_alt: Two bars: the value of a benchmark forecast and of a forecast 10% lower, both discounted at the same benchmark rate, with the valuation ratio K, the gain of capital and the effective rate
tools.paper: From Unified Discounting to Dual-Risk: A New Lens on DCF Valuation
